summary: This informational RFC describes use cases for Seamless BFD and gives requirements for protocol mechanisms that simplify detecting forwarding failures. S-BFD removes much of BFD's negotiation, which speeds up session establishment.

plainLanguage.summary: Situations where checking quickly whether a network path still works helps, and what that checking needs.

questions: why use seamless bfd instead of regular bfd
how does s-bfd simplify network operations
subtitle: Use cases for simplified failure detection that starts immediately without negotiation.

tldr.problem: BFD sessions require exchange of discriminator values and initialization handshakes before they can detect failures, causing delay when operators need to quickly verify new network paths, especially with software-defined networks creating paths dynamically.
tldr.mechanism: Seamless BFD (S-BFD) eliminates the handshake by pre-assigning BFD discriminators to network entities, allowing failure detection to begin immediately upon sending the first packet without prior negotiation.
tldr.outcome: Enables rapid validation of newly-created network paths, centralized control of network paths, and simplified BFD deployment in dynamic networks and segment routing systems.

facts.label: BFD discriminator
facts.value: Unique identifier for a BFD session, allocated by endpoints

facts.label: Protocol number for BFD
facts.value: IP protocol 17 (same as UDP in some deployments)

today: RFC 7882 is an Informational RFC published in July 2016 describing use cases and requirements for Seamless BFD. The actual protocol mechanisms are defined in companion RFCs 7880 (general S-BFD) and 7881 (S-BFD for IPv4, IPv6, and MPLS). S-BFD has been adopted in production networks and is particularly used in segment routing deployments and SDN-controlled networks.

sections.title: The Need for Seamless Failure Detection
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), defined in RFC 5880, is a lightweight protocol for detecting forwarding failures. A router sends BFD packets to a neighbor, and if it stops receiving responses, it declares the path down and triggers recovery.

However, traditional BFD has a setup phase. Two endpoints must exchange BFD discriminators (unique session identifiers) before either one starts monitoring the path. This exchange can take seconds, creating a gap between when a path is created and when failure detection begins.

This delay becomes problematic when networks create paths dynamically. In Software-Defined Networks (SDN), a controller creates traffic-engineered tunnels on demand. Before using a new tunnel for real traffic, operators want to validate it with BFD. Traditional BFD's setup delay means the controller cannot immediately verify path validity.

Seamless BFD (S-BFD) solves this by pre-allocating BFD discriminators. If a centralized entity (controller or operator) assigns each router a BFD discriminator in advance, routers know exactly which discriminator to use for any target. They can send the first BFD packet immediately without negotiation, beginning failure detection at once.
sections.plainLanguage: With regular BFD, two devices must have a handshake before checking if they're connected. S-BFD pre-assigns identifying numbers so they can start checking without the handshake, saving time.

sections.title: Unidirectional Monitoring and Validation
sections.content:
Not all network paths require bidirectional validation. Static routes, unidirectional MPLS LSPs, and segment routing paths are inherently one-way: they only need to verify reachability in the forward direction. With traditional BFD, even unidirectional paths require setting up bidirectional sessions and provisioning both endpoints.

S-BFD enables true unidirectional monitoring: a source can send BFD packets to a target without requiring the target to maintain session state for the reverse direction. The target responds to BFD packets using whatever path is available (which may be different from the forward path), but no bidirectional session is established.

This reduces operational complexity for unidirectional paths. The source node provisions itself and knows what discriminator to use. The target node needs only to listen for packets destined to its pre-assigned discriminator and respond; no session configuration is needed at the target.

This use case is particularly valuable for segment routing, where paths are often unidirectional and created dynamically by a central controller. The controller can immediately insert BFD checks without provisioning reverse-path session state at targets.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only need to check that traffic flows one direction (like checking if a tunnel is working), you don't need to set up a two-way conversation. S-BFD lets one side check without the other side being configured.

sections.title: Rapid Validation Before Switching Traffic
sections.content:
When new traffic-engineered paths are created, operators want to validate that they work before switching live traffic onto them. With traditional BFD, this validation cannot begin until the handshake completes, which can take seconds. During this delay, traffic cannot use the path, extending service downtime or delaying service activation.

S-BFD allows immediate validation: the moment a path is created, BFD packets can flow without negotiation. The target receives the packet, recognizes its pre-assigned discriminator, and responds. The source immediately knows the path is working and traffic can switch.

This is critical in SDN deployments where a controller creates dozens or hundreds of paths in response to traffic patterns. Rapid validation ensures the controller can use new paths quickly, improving load balancing and reducing blackholing risks.

Three-way handshakes and LSP ping bootstrapping that traditional BFD requires become bottlenecks in large-scale dynamic networks. Eliminating this negotiation phase is essential for modern, software-driven network operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine building a new highway and needing to check it works before opening it to traffic. Regular BFD requires weeks of setup meetings before you can run a test car. S-BFD lets you test the moment it's built.

sections.title: Advanced Use Cases: Centralized Control and Anycast
sections.content:
Centralized Traffic Engineering: A network controller manages all path creation and traffic steering. When the controller creates a new path, it immediately needs to verify it. With S-BFD, the controller can query any path without prior arrangement with the network nodes. Nodes simply accept BFD packets destined to their assigned discriminators and respond. The controller scales to monitor hundreds of paths without configuration state at each endpoint.

Segment Routing Monitoring: Segment Routing (SR) is increasingly deployed in SDN environments. Each segment (portion of a path) can be independently monitored with S-BFD from a central controller. The controller assigns discriminators to segments and performs liveness checks, enabling granular monitoring of the segment routing domain.

Anycast Monitoring: Anycast addresses have multiple servers responding. Traditional BFD cannot handle this because it requires specific bidirectional session state between two endpoints. S-BFD allows a source to send BFD packets to an anycast address, and whichever server receives the packet responds. No session state is needed at servers that don't receive packets.

ECMP Path Validation: Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) uses multiple parallel paths. When paths change (due to link failures or dynamic routing), BFD sessions may be invalidated. S-BFD allows establishing a separate session for each ECMP path without complex bootstrapping via MPLS Echo Request, simplifying deployment and reducing overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: S-BFD works well when a central controller manages all paths, when you need to monitor individual segments of a path separately, when multiple servers share one address, or when there are many equal-cost alternate paths.

sections.title: Requirements and Security Considerations
sections.content:
S-BFD requirements include:

  • Targets must process S-BFD packets based on received discriminators and send responses if context is found
  • Sources must establish unidirectional sessions without bidirectional handshakes
  • Session parameters (transmission intervals, reception intervals) must be modifiable without changing session state
  • S-BFD should support fault isolation capability when faults are detected
  • Multiple S-BFD sessions must be possible between the same pair of endpoints (useful for ECMP monitoring)
  • Robust protection against loop attacks and security threats must be incorporated

Security considerations are important. Because S-BFD eliminates negotiation, misconfiguration could result in BFD packets sent to wrong nodes. However, nodes not expecting S-BFD packets simply discard them (no S-BFD context found), and nodes with S-BFD enabled discard packets with discriminator mismatches. S-BFD should not reduce security compared to traditional BFD; protocol extensions (RFC 7880, RFC 7881) address security considerations in detail.
sections.plainLanguage: S-BFD needs to support simple one-way checks, changing how often packets are sent without restarting the check, finding exactly where failures happen, and protecting against misconfiguration and attacks.
